short_title: Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel (Resolution)
full_title: HACIENDA SAN ISIDRO / SILOS FARMS AND REY SILOS LLAMADO, PETITIONERS, VS. LUCITO VILLARUEL AND HELEN VILLARUEL, RESPONDENTS.
subject: Labor Law and Social Legislation
syllabus_topic: III. Employment Relationship > A. Employer-Employee Relationship > 2. Determination of Employer-Employee Relationship > a. Fourfold Test
topics: Control test: right to control both the end and the manner and means
Burden on the claimant to prove control by substantial evidence
Art. 295 is not a test for the existence of an employment relationship
Gapayao v. Fulo's reading of Mercado and its application of the control test corrected
Requisites for regular seasonal employment maintained

other_subjects.subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: III. Civil Procedure > S. Post-judgment Remedies > 5. Appeal and Review > e. Modes > v. Appeal by Certiorari to SC (Rule 45)

doctrine:
On the employer's motion for reconsideration, the Court **maintained** the two requisites for regular seasonal employment laid down in its November 13, 2023 Decision: (1) seasonal work or services; and (2) employment for more than one season. It also kept the rule that pakyaw pay does not negate regular employment if the employer has the right to control. It nonetheless **set aside the Decision and reversed the CA**, because the worker never proved that right.

**Under the control test, the employer must reserve the right to control not only the end achieved but also the manner and means used to reach it. The worker claiming benefits bears the burden of proving that right by substantial evidence, and the control must be of a level that interferes with the means and methods of accomplishing the assigned tasks.** Rules that merely serve as guidelines toward a mutually desired result, without dictating means and methods, do not establish an employment relationship. The fact that a person works on the alleged employer's farm does not automatically mean the farm owner controlled, or reserved the right to control, the means and methods of the work. The Court clarified *Gapayao v. Fulo* on two points:
- *Gapayao* applied the control test incompletely. It presumed control from farm ownership and the right to review the quality of output, which shows control of the end only.
- *Gapayao* misappreciated *Mercado*. Freedom to offer services to other farm owners was merely an added observation of the Labor Arbiter in *Mercado*, not its ratio decidendi. *Mercado* rested on on-and-off hiring.

**Art. 295 (formerly Art. 280) of the Labor Code is not a criterion for determining whether an employer-employee relationship exists.** It only distinguishes regular from casual employees, and it does not apply where the relationship itself is disputed. The following do not by themselves prove employment: length of service, repeated assignment of tasks, and receipt of wages, which is only one prong of the four-fold test. In a Rule 45 petition, uniform factual findings of the LA, NLRC and CA bind the Court only if supported by substantial evidence. Factual review is allowed in exceptional cases.
facts:
In its November 13, 2023 Decision, the Court denied petitioners' Rule 45 petition and affirmed the CA's January 9, 2015 Amended Decision, which declared respondent Helen Villaruel a regular seasonal employee of Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms. The Decision held that she met the requisites for regular seasonal employment. It held that her freedom to work elsewhere and her pakyaw pay did not matter. It also held that petitioners "could easily exercise control" over her because she worked on their hacienda.

Petitioners moved for reconsideration. They argued as follows:
- They had no control over the manner by which Helen did her work, and the finding of control rested on an unfounded assumption that they could easily supervise her.
- She was free to contract her services with other employers.
- *Hacienda Fatima* did not distinguish between workers hired on and off for a single phase and workers hired repeatedly for the same phases, so the Court erred in holding *Mercado* inapplicable.

Respondents opposed the motion as pro forma for raising no new matter.

The record of the lower tribunals stood as follows. The NLRC first held (September 30, 2011) that Helen was not an employee, then reversed itself on January 27, 2012. The CA first held (March 27, 2013) that she was not an employee for failure to prove control, then reversed itself in its January 9, 2015 Amended Decision. In their Position Paper, petitioners had disputed the very existence of an employer-employee relationship.
issues: Whether the Court may review the lower tribunals' factual finding that petitioners had the right to control Helen's work.

Whether Hacienda Fatima distinguished workers hired on and off for any single phase from those hired repeatedly for the same phases, and whether freedom to contract with other employers by itself negates regular seasonal employment.
Whether Helen proved by substantial evidence that petitioners had the right to control the manner and means of her work.
ruling:
**1. Yes, the factual finding may be reviewed.** Petitioners' claim that they lacked control raises a question of fact, which is generally beyond a Rule 45 petition. The rule has exceptions, however. Examples include findings grounded entirely on speculation, surmises or conjectures; inferences that are manifestly mistaken, absurd or impossible; grave abuse of discretion; and judgments based on a misapprehension of facts. These exceptions were present. The Court rejected petitioners' claim that the LA, NLRC and CA did not uniformly find Helen a regular employee. The NLRC and the CA each reversed themselves, so in the end all three found her regular. But uniform findings bind the Court only if supported by substantial evidence, and here they were not.

**2. Hacienda Fatima did draw the distinction, but freedom to work elsewhere is not decisive.** *Hacienda Fatima* held *Mercado* inapplicable because the *Mercado* workers "were not hired regularly and repeatedly for the same phase/s of agricultural work, but on and off for any single phase thereof." That holding plainly distinguishes the two kinds of workers. *Gapayao*, which petitioners invoked, "misappreciated *Mercado, Sr.*" In *Mercado*, the workers' freedom to offer their services to other farm owners was merely an added observation of the LA, whose findings the Court found supported by evidence. That freedom was not the ratio decidendi. *Mercado* rested on the on-and-off nature of the hiring, and the freedom to work elsewhere was merely the logical result of that hiring.

**3. No, Helen did not prove the right of control, so the CA erred.** The control test requires the right to control both the end achieved and the manner and means of reaching it. It requires the existence of the right, not its exercise. *Gapayao* stated the test correctly, but it "incompletely applied the test." It found only that the farm owner could review the quality of the work, which is control of the result, and made no finding on the manner and means. Even if petitioners could be presumed to have the right to review Helen's output, the right to control the manner and means could not be presumed. Helen had the burden of proving it by substantial evidence, and she failed.

None of the tribunals below found such control:
- The LA relied on the nature of Helen's work and her length of service. But "length of service and the repeated act of assigning tasks do not automatically result in entitlement to the rights and privileges of a regular employee."
- The NLRC relied on her work at the farm since 1978 and her receipt of wages. But receipt of wages "is but one prong in the four-fold test and is not a conclusive factor."
- The CA relied on Art. 280 (now 295). But that article "should not be used as a criterion to determine the existence of an employer-employee relationship," and it does not apply where the relationship is disputed, as it was here. The CA wrongly stated that petitioners never denied that Helen was an employee. They disputed it in their Position Paper, and the LA acknowledged the dispute.

Control must be of a level that interferes with the means and methods of the work. Guidelines toward a mutually desired result do not suffice. The CA therefore "seriously erred" in not finding grave abuse of discretion by the NLRC, whose findings lacked substantial evidence. The Court quoted *Javier v. Fly Ace Corp.*: social justice does not mean "that every labor dispute will be automatically decided in favor of labor," and management's rights are also entitled to respect.
disposition: The Motion for Reconsideration was GRANTED. The Court SET ASIDE its November 13, 2023 Decision and rendered a new one GRANTING the Petition for Review on Certiorari. It REVERSED and SET ASIDE the CA's January 9, 2015 Amended Decision and July 20, 2015 Resolution in CA-G.R. SP No. 07025. Gesmundo, C.J. (Chairperson), Hernando, Zalameda and Marquez, JJ. concurred.

bar_questions.q: Lina filed an illegal dismissal complaint against Finca Verde, a sugarcane farm. She alleged that she had worked on the farm every milling season since 1990, planting and weeding, and was paid per task. Finca Verde denied that she was ever its employee. The Labor Arbiter, the NLRC and the Court of Appeals (on certiorari) all ruled that she was a regular employee. They reasoned that her work was necessary or desirable to the farm's business, that she had worked for many seasons, and that she received wages from the farm. None of them found that Finca Verde had the right to control how she did her tasks, and the record has no evidence on that point. On Finca Verde's Rule 45 petition, should the Supreme Court sustain the finding that Lina was a regular employee?

alac.answer: No. Lina failed to prove an employer-employee relationship, because she offered no substantial evidence that Finca Verde had the right to control the manner and means of her work.
alac.legal_basis: Under the control test, the employer must reserve the right to control not only the end achieved but also the manner and means of reaching it. The worker claiming the benefits must prove that right by substantial evidence. Art. 295 of the Labor Code is not a criterion for determining whether an employment relationship exists, and it does not apply where the relationship is disputed. Length of service and repeated assignment of tasks do not automatically make one a regular employee. Receipt of wages is only one prong of the four-fold test. (Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel, G.R. No. 220087, August 11, 2025, Resolution.)
alac.application: Finca Verde denied the existence of any employment relationship, so the threshold issue is whether Lina was an employee at all. The tribunals relied on Art. 295, which presupposes an employment relationship and so cannot be used to prove one. They also relied on her years of service and her wages, but neither proves control. No tribunal found, and no evidence shows, that Finca Verde could dictate how Lina planted or weeded. That she worked on the farm does not mean the farm controlled her means and methods. Because the uniform findings rest on no substantial evidence of control, they do not bind the Court, and the CA erred in not finding grave abuse of discretion by the NLRC.
alac.conclusion: The Supreme Court should reverse the finding that Lina was a regular employee, because the right of control was not proved.

bar_questions.q: Assume instead that Lina presented the farm's written instructions. They fix the depth and spacing of canepoints, the weeding method, and the daily schedule, and they authorize the farm's overseer to reassign or correct workers who deviate. The overseer rarely inspected her work. Lina was paid on a pakyaw basis, was hired every season for the same planting and weeding tasks, and in the off-season worked on neighboring farms. Is Lina a regular employee?

alac.answer: Yes. Lina is a regular seasonal employee of Finca Verde.
alac.legal_basis: A seasonal employee is regular if (1) the work or services are seasonal in nature and (2) the employee is employed for that work for more than one season. Pakyaw pay does not negate regular employment if the employer has the right to control. The control test requires only the existence of the right to control the end and the manner and means, not its actual exercise. Freedom to offer services to other farm owners does not by itself negate regular status. In Mercado, that freedom was merely an added observation of the Labor Arbiter, and the ruling rested on on-and-off hiring. (Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel, G.R. No. 220087, August 11, 2025, Resolution, maintaining the November 13, 2023 Decision on these points.)
alac.application: The written instructions dictate how the work is done (depth, spacing, method and schedule), and the overseer may correct deviations. This is control over the manner and means, not mere guidelines toward a result, and it is proven by documents. It does not matter that the overseer seldom inspected, because the right need not be exercised. With the employment relationship established, Lina meets both requisites: planting and weeding are seasonal, and she was hired for the same tasks every season. Her pakyaw pay is only a method of computing wages. Her off-season work on other farms does not matter, because she was hired repeatedly for the same tasks, not on and off for single phases.
alac.conclusion: Lina is a regular seasonal employee because the right of control is proven and both requisites are present.

bar_questions.q: In a farm worker's case, the Labor Arbiter, the NLRC and the CA all found an employer-employee relationship. The employer filed a Rule 45 petition with the Supreme Court. The worker's counsel argues that (a) the uniform factual findings of the three tribunals are binding on the Supreme Court and cannot be reviewed under Rule 45, and (b) under the constitutional policy of social justice and full protection to labor, any doubt must be resolved in the worker's favor, so the employer's petition must fail. Rule on both arguments.

alac.answer: (a) Not necessarily. Uniform findings bind the Court only if supported by substantial evidence, and the Court may review facts in recognized exceptional cases. (b) No. Social justice does not mean that every labor dispute is automatically decided in favor of labor.
alac.legal_basis: Only questions of law are generally raised under Rule 45. This rule admits of exceptions, such as when the conclusion is grounded entirely on speculation, surmises or conjectures; when the inference is manifestly mistaken, absurd or impossible; when there is grave abuse of discretion; or when the judgment is based on a misapprehension of facts. The principle that uniform factual findings of labor tribunals bind the Court applies only if the findings are supported by substantial evidence. Quoting Javier v. Fly Ace Corp., the Court held that the policy of social justice does not mean "that every labor dispute will be automatically decided in favor of labor." Management also has rights entitled to respect, and justice is for the deserving, in light of the established facts and the applicable law. (Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel, G.R. No. 220087, August 11, 2025, Resolution.)
alac.application: (a) If the tribunals found an employment relationship without substantial evidence of the right to control, their findings rest on conjecture or a misapprehension of facts. The Court may then review and reverse them despite their uniformity. (b) The worker still bears the burden of proving the employment relationship by substantial evidence. The pro-labor policy does not relieve her of that burden or allow the Court to presume control. If the evidence fails, the employer's petition should be granted.
alac.conclusion: Neither the uniformity of the findings nor the social justice policy shields the ruling from reversal when the employment relationship was not proven by substantial evidence.

notes: Cross-reference: this Resolution sets aside Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel, G.R. No. 220087, November 13, 2023 (case id gr-220087-20231113). It keeps that Decision's doctrine on the two requisites for regular seasonal employment and on pakyaw workers, but reverses the result. Doubt: the fallo reverses and sets aside the CA Amended Decision and Resolution in full and does not say what ruling replaces them or expressly dispose of Helen's complaint. The Rule 45 petition had assailed the CA only insofar as it declared Helen a regular employee and awarded her backwages and separation pay. The CA Amended Decision also contained rulings on Lucito (just dismissal, money awards, and attorney's fees for both spouses), which the Resolution does not discuss. The Resolution also does not rule expressly on respondents' objection that the motion was pro forma.
